description: FlameFinder is an SI-powered web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's PSI database plus 68 NTRS abstracts. summary: FlameFinder is an SI-powered web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, together with 68 published NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) abstracts that report their results. For a chosen crew environment (spacecraft cabin, 10.2 psia vehicle, lunar base or pressurized rover at 34% oxygen, or a pure-oxygen spacesuit) it ranks the studies, gives an SI summary and the key findings of each, extracts 58 numbers for predictive modelling with CSV and JSON export, and turns results into guidance for prevention, detection, suppression and material choice. Every SI item carries a verbatim NASA quote that a script checks, so nothing unsupported reaches the user. It also finds a gap: no fabric or plastic in PSI has a stated flame test at lunar-base air. And it carries space fire data back to Earth: smoke detection in submarines, safer materials in buildings and aircraft, and cleaner engines.
details:
What it does

FlameFinder answers one question for a mission designer, researcher or student: which NASA microgravity combustion results apply to the air my crew will breathe and the materials they will live with, and what did those experiments find? The user picks a crew environment, the fuel type of concern (solids such as fabrics and plastics, liquid droplets, or gases) and the fire-safety pillar (prevent, detect, suppress). FlameFinder then guides the user through seven tabs, each opening with a short "how to use this tab" and "what it means" box written for non-specialists:

·       1 Start here: what FlameFinder is, the main discovery, what each tab does and where SI is used.

·       2 Best studies: all 24 PSI combustion investigations ranked for the chosen crew home, fuel and safety focus, each with an SI summary, its key published findings with NTRS links, quoted NASA sentences and an orange "Add to compare list" button.

·       3 Compare: up to three studies side by side, with an automatic same-and-different box plus hardware, sensors, sample or burner, what varied, what stayed fixed, fuels, oxygen, pressure, flow and findings.

·       4 Find the test gap: each investigation's stated oxygen and pressure range against four crew atmospheres, including ACME CFI-G at up to 85% oxygen.

·       5 Helps on Earth: Earth problems the data helps solve, such as fire suppression in sealed spaces, smoke detectors for submarines and underwater laboratories, material flammability in buildings, aircraft and oxygen-rich rooms, soot pollution and engine efficiency, building on the challenge's own examples of fine water mist extinguishers, smoke detection and firefighter gear.

·       6 Ask a question: plain-English questions answered with sentences quoted from PSI records and NTRS abstracts, each telling the user which experiment and which part of the record holds the answer. A purple SI box sums them up in 50 to 70 plain words, with each [number] linking to the NASA sentence it rests on.

·       7 Science & data: Numbers & safety advice (58 numbers for predictive modelling, such as extinction temperatures, oxygen limits, quenching flow speeds and sample sizes, each with units, conditions and its NASA quote, exportable as CSV or JSON, plus 44 control implications grouped as prevent ignition, detect early, suppress and choose safer materials); Gravity & hardware (no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI yet, LUCI and FM2 expected, the ACME E-FIELD stand-in, 19 NASA results comparing microgravity with normal gravity as bounds for the Moon and Mars, hardware families, and the SAME smoke instrument reused for dust in DAFT); and How it works (formula, SI pipeline, sources, limits).

What we found

PSI lists three NASA-considered cabin atmospheres (14.7 psia at 21%, 10.2 psia at 26.5%, 8.2 psia at 34% oxygen, quoted in the ACME BRE record). Only ACME BRE (gaseous flames on a burner that emulates a burning solid) and FLEX-2 (fuel droplets, 0.5 to 3.0 atm, 10 to 40% oxygen) state test conditions that cover the 34% oxygen, 56.5 kPa lunar-base atmosphere. CFI-G reached up to 85% oxygen but burned gases. None of the flown solid-material studies (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire-I to III) states a test at that atmosphere in PSI. In NASA's open archive, the fabrics and plastics a lunar crew will live with have no stated flame test at the air they will breathe. We present this as an archive finding, not a claim about all NASA testing.

How it works

·       Data: scripts/build_dataset.py pulls all PSI combustion records through the public PSI search API. scripts/fetch_findings.py pulls NTRS abstracts for each investigation; we reviewed relevance by hand and removed papers belonging to a different flight.

·       SI layer: scripts/si_build.py sends each PSI record and up to four abstracts to a large language model (Claude Haiku 5.5 through OpenRouter) and asks for a summary, findings, numbers, controls, Earth applications, test variables, sensors and sample geometry. Every item must include a verbatim NASA quote. The script checks each quote against the source and deletes items whose quote is missing or whose number is not inside the quote: 393 items kept, 7 deleted. The model runs at build time only, so no key ships with the site; the full build cost about US$0.04.

·       Ranking: Okapi BM25 retrieval plus a weighted score (0.30 text relevance, 0.20 safety pillar, 0.20 atmosphere match, 0.15 fuel type, 0.15 evidence strength).

·       Front end: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with hand-drawn SVG, no external libraries, hosted on GitHub Pages.

Benefits

·       Engineers find the relevant flight data and results for a habitat atmosphere in minutes, with numbers ready for flammability models.

·       Researchers see which conditions NASA has and has not tested, which points to the next experiment, and how microgravity and normal-gravity results bound the Moon and Mars.

·       Every SI statement sits next to its NASA quote and source link, so the tool supports expert review instead of replacing it.

·       Earth: the same data informs smoke detectors, suppression systems, safer materials and cleaner combustion.

What we hope to achieve

We want FlameFinder to be a front door to PSI combustion data and to make the 34% oxygen solid-material gap visible to the people who plan the next flight experiments. Next steps: ingest PSI data files (flame spread rates, extinction points) where access allows, add partial-gravity data from LUCI and FM2 when it reaches PSI, and validate the ranking with combustion researchers.

Tools

Python 3, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG; NASA PSI search API; NASA NTRS API; OpenRouter with Claude Haiku 5.5 for the build-time SI layer; GitHub Pages; Playwright and ffmpeg for the demo video; Kokoro TTS for narration.
